articles.title_orig: CNN, MS NOW and Politico allowed back at the White House after judge blocked Trump’s ban
articles.title_zh: CNN, MS NOW and Politico allowed back at the White House after judge blocked Trump’s ban
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were allowed back at the White House Thursday, nearly a week after President Donald Trump banned them. The reinstatement came after a judged ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access.
White House reporters Betsy Klein of CNN and Laura Barrón-López of MS NOW immediately began reporting live on the air after they were allowed onto the White House grounds Thursday afternoon. Both media outlets pointed to the on-air reporting when asked for comment. Politico wrote shortly afterward that one of its reporters was granted access, too.
The media outlets scored a victory overnight when U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly reinstated the outlets’ access for 14 days while their legal challenge proceeded.
Yet on Thursday morning, reporters from the banned outlets were still prohibited from entering the White House. Shortly after, Kelly then ordered the administration to respond in writing by 12:30 p.m. after journalists from the three media outlets were turned away. After receiving Stopperich’s filing, the judge denied the news organizations’ request for an emergency hearing.
It was not clear why the journalists were initially still barred from entering. The White House did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.
In the administration’s court filing shortly before the deadline, White House press operations director Micah Stopperich presented a timeline the administration’s activity to reinstate the journalists’ access.
Stopperich said her team was told at shortly after 7 a.m. to restore access “to affected reporters by turning on their hard badges,” and soon after, they began to do so. Secret Service indicated shortly after 9 a.m. that the journalists’ passes were “back on,” and they were dropped off at the entry gate for pick up within the hour.
Trump announced his ban on the three news outlets in a post on Truth Social on Friday, saying it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
Kelly wrote in his temporary restraining order that Trump’s directive was most likely unconstitutional. He wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their lawsuit against the administration, at least on the grounds that their credentials were revoked last week without due process.
Trump, the judge wrote, did not dispute that the outlets “did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked.”
“This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action,” the attorney representing the news outlets, Ted Boutrous, said in a statement.
Thursday’s order rejected the White House’s argument that banning the outlets was motivated by national security concerns , saying the administration offered little proof to back up the claim.
“Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote.
Inside lawsuit challenging Trump's White House outlet ban
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office a short time after the post, Trump referred to his directive as “the ban on the free press.”
“I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said .
He said the policy was not in response to a particular report, but because of “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets said in their suit challenging the ban that Trump’s remarks show the policy was motivated by “retaliation” and “intended to cow” the outlets “into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate.”
In letters to the news outlets on Tuesday, the White House accused them of publishing “sensitive security information, and misinformation,” which “undermines the President’s ability to safeguard the national security.”
The White House cited specific articles about munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia, as well as one about a request for $1 billion in funding for East Wing renovations that the president had said would be fully funded by donors, and another about negative “ vibes ” at the recent Republican midterm convention.
Addressing the “extraordinary” standard that the government argued gave it the right to revoke the outlets’ passes without prior notice, Kelly wrote that the sorts of stories cited in the letters “are routine,” and stretch back months or even years.
NBC News previously reported that Trump’s Friday announcement caught a number of high-level White House aides off guard. A senior White House official defended the move to NBC News earlier this week, saying: “Nobody close to the President was surprised at his action to hold the fake news accountable.”
The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents’ Association and a group of 49 news and media organizations — including NBCUniversal Media LLC, the parent company of NBC News — filed a legal brief in the case Wednesday backing the three outlets.
The filing said the president’s stated reasons for the ban “are transparently viewpoint discriminatory” and “inconsistent with the First Amendment.”
“The ban at issue in this case does exactly what longstanding D.C. Circuit precedent” has said the government can’t do, the filing said — “prohibited three news organizations from access to the entirety of the White House and its grounds due to the content of their reporting.”
It also clashes, the filing said, “with bedrock Supreme Court precedent, which recognizes that ‘even though a person has no ‘right’ to a valuable governmental benefit,’ the government ‘may not deny a benefit to a person on a basis that infringes his constitutionally protected interests — especially, his interest in freedom of speech.’”

articles.title_orig: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs but oil prices buffeted by Iran headlines
articles.title_zh: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs but oil prices buffeted by Iran headlines
articles.content_orig:
Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday, as the price of oil jumped to as high as $108 per barrel.
The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared as high as 5.446%, a level not seen in 22 years.
After posting its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond continued advancing on Thursday. In early trading it climbed as high as 5.168%. That remains its highest level since 2007.
Due to the influence that the 10-year yield has over consumer borrowing rates, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.37% on Thursday, its highest level since May 2024.
Meanwhile, oil prices jumped again overnight after a mediated U.S. dialogue with Iran at the United Nations General Assembly produced no tangible evidence of any progress toward ending the seven-month war.
Yet much of the day’s gains in oil were reversed shortly after midday Eastern time, following a Reuters report that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path out of the war. The path reportedly involves Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters’ multiple unnamed sources.
NBC News has not confirmed the Reuters report.
International Brent crude oil was still up by 2.5% to over $105 per barrel, however, while U.S. crude oil was still up more than 2% at more than $94 per barrel.
Since the start of the year, both Brent and West Texas Intermediary crude are up more than 60%.
Those rising oil prices have continued to push commercial diesel fuel prices to all-time records. On Thursday, the national average price for diesel was $4.51, effectively unchanged from a day earlier, but up 73% since the Iran war began.
Likewise, the national average price of regular unleaded gas was 50% higher Thursday than it when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, at $4.48 per gallon.
Stocks fell in early trading, but like oil, turned sharply upwards on the Reuters report. The S&P 500 erased a drop of 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite erased a 0.9% slip. Both indexes were trading flat around 1 p.m. ET.
Around the world, the bond sell-off is roiling sovereign debt markets.
“The acceleration higher in US rates yesterday is being felt globally as to highlight for the umpteenth time that we’re all in this global bond boat together,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth.
The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond rose to its highest level since 1996 on Thursday, while Germany’s 10-year bund notched its highest yield since 2009.
“As summer officially ends, macro data are still fairly solid in the US, as indicated by a 4%-type unemployment rate and 2%-ish growth,” wrote Bank of America’s global rates analysts.
“But the risks continue to pile up for anxious markets,” they added, pointing to ongoing trade wars, the energy supply shock, upcoming midterm elections and potential risks to the AI boom.
One major driver of the surge in bond yields this week was a report from S&P Global, released Wednesday morning, that found that while U.S. business activity accelerated in September, “firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher.”
That led investors and traders to ramp up their bets on Fed rate hikes.
Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said the central bank still has more work to do to help bring down inflation.
It’s “likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year,” Williams said during a speech in London Thursday.
Nonetheless, he said, the U.S. economy has demonstrated “remarkable resilience” in the face of “significant shocks” hitting it.
Another key official, Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed , said Thursday that she too expects “some modest further tightening may be warranted.”
In central banker parlance, tightening refers to raising rates.
The rise in bond yields has continued despite a series of measures taken — and warnings delivered — by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month.
“ I am the house now, ” Bessent said on Sept. 8, “and you can bet against me if you want.”
At the time, Bessent was defending a Treasury Department intervention to help prop up the Japanese yen. The hope was that a stronger yen would relieve pressure on the Japanese government to sell U.S. Treasury bonds.
But it hasn’t entirely worked, and as of Thursday, the Japanese yen had again weakened to levels on par with it’s exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from early September.
Bessent has also intervened in the U.S. bond markets, buying back longer-dated Treasurys in an effort to keep their yields low.
The next test for Bessent’s plan will arrive later on Thursday, when the Treasury Department is set to buy back up to $6 billion worth of 20- to 30-year bonds.
In response to the department’s initial buyback earlier this month, bond yields rose — exactly the opposite reaction from what the administration intended.
But Bessent has brushed off the stumble, insisting that the U.S. bond market is still the “best performing” in the world and crediting President Donald Trump for it.
“If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” Bessent said in an interview on Sept. 10.
But not everyone is entirely convinced by Bessent’s swagger.
“US Treasury Secretary ‘House’ Bessent seems to be demonstrating the house does not always win,” wrote Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, on Thursday morning.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: US citizen injured in Illinois after ICE agents mistook him for fugitive and tried to arrest him
articles.title_zh: US citizen injured in Illinois after ICE agents mistook him for fugitive and tried to arrest him
articles.content_orig:
Man left bloodied and hurt after immigration enforcement agents tried to arrest him in Evanston, a Chicago suburb
An eyewitness has described how two federal immigration agents allegedly beat and badly injured a US citizen in a botched arrest attempt in Illinois , and left the man dazed and bleeding on the ground as they walked away after realizing their apparent mistake.
Bystander Ryan Garton told the Associated Press that he saw the agents pinning down the man, who is Black, on the side of the road as he was driving home on Sunday in Evanston, a suburb of Chicago. He said he pulled over to record what was happening on video.
“His upper right eye socket and temple were swollen as if he had been punched,” Garton said. The man’s face, he added, was scraped “as if it had been ground into the sidewalk”.
Garton, 56, said one agent had his knee on the man’s back and was “beating up on him”, even as the person shouted: “I’m a citizen, leave me alone.” The witness said about five people were standing nearby, yelling at the agents to stop.
Garton said he urged the officer to get off the man so he could inspect his injuries, and also asserted that the officer acknowledged that he was already aware the man was a US citizen. When the agent stepped away, Garton said he saw bloodstains in the shape of handprints on the man’s shirt.
The man told Garton that he had been walking to a pharmacy to pick up a prescription when the agents stopped him.
Another eyewitness, Michael Lipson, the owner of a store across the street from where the incident occurred, said he saw the federal officers wrestle the man to the ground as the alleged victim repeatedly yelled that he was a citizen. The man’s face looked “badly messed up”, Lipson told the AP.
Lipson said the officers checked cards and papers from the man’s wallet before leaving them scattered on the road. Lipson said he laid out his sweatshirt for the man to rest on while Garton inspected his injuries.
Authorities in Illinois said earlier this week they were looking into the incident , which ended with the victim in hospital with injuries to his head, neck and teeth. It also left one of the agents with a bloodied hand that he told Evanston police he sustained while the suspect resisted an effort to handcuff him.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees the Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) agency, said in a statement that ICE officers had “encountered an individual who resembled the target” of an enforcement operation.
“The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself,” the statement said, adding that the agents “left the scene without further incident” after the man said who he was.
“When ICE officers offered the individual assistance, he refused.”
More detailed accounts of the confrontation, which took place at about 10am on Sunday, have come mostly from the city’s police department and local officials.

A police statement said the alleged victim told officers that he received head, face and neck injuries during the beating. It said the agents walked away because they claimed a crowd had gathered and they feared protesters would attack them.
Daniel Biss, the Democratic mayor of Evanston, said in a post on X that the man was treated at St Francis hospital for minor injuries, and that the city’s police department “continues to investigate the situation, and we will remain vigilant about federal activities”.
In a separate post on Wednesday, Biss condemned Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, which has escalated through the president’s second term with enforcement “surges” into Democratic-run cities and states in particular , and resulted in a record 50,000 arrests in July alone.
“This violence must end. We need to take Evanston’s energy and fight to Washington to abolish ICE, hold the Trump administration accountable, and end the funding of these brutal invasions into our cities,” Biss wrote.
The incident was one of three separate violent events Sunday involving federal immigration officers. In Austin, Texas, an ICE agent shot and seriously wounded a 28-year-old Venezuelan man in a traffic stop while he worked as a DoorDash delivery driver.
In Michigan, authorities are investigating the death of a 36-year-old Guatemalan national who crashed his car into a tree at high speed after reportedly attempting to flee immigration officers that were trying to detain him.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Denmark expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in coming months, intelligence service says
articles.title_zh: Denmark expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in coming months, intelligence service says
articles.content_orig:
Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.
In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine , or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.
The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.
Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.
Gawkowski said it had not been established who ​was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack.
“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.
Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.
Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.
In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.
A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.
“Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.
“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.
The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.
The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.
The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.
There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.
Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.
Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations
articles.title_zh: Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations
articles.content_orig:
Macklemore announced he will launch the Free Palestine Tour this fall after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour this month over his pro-Palestinian performance .
The “Thrift Shop” rapper took to Instagram on Monday and jokingly said that his “schedule freed up a bit,” announcing three performance dates in Dublin, London and Paris next month.
“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage,” he wrote. “When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”
The performances are part of what Macklemore named the “Free Palestine” tour and the poster said it would be him “and friends.” He said he spent the last week reaching out to other artists to work out scheduling, but no other names have been announced as of Monday.
He wrote that there has been a “been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation” and the expectations of artists.
“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” Macklemore said. “People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community.”
All proceeds from the performances would benefit organizations supporting Palestinians, he said.
Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, announced earlier this month that U.S. venues gave Sheeran an ultimatum to remove him from the tour or face show cancelations. Macklemore said that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft “rallied” other stadium owners after taking issue with his “Free Palestine” remarks during a show.
Sheeran confirmed that Kraft was among those who called him after Macklemore performed his anti-war song and the speech that preceded it at Metlife Stadium circulated online.
The situation surrounding Macklemore, Sheeran and Kraft made international headlines this month as many debated not just Macklemore’s speech regarding the Israel-Gaza war, but also the rights for artists to express their views.
It began when Macklemore joined Sheeran’s “Loop” tour in New Jersey and performed “Hind’s Hall,” his song inspired by the anti-war protests at Columbia University in 2024. Macklemore made a speech prior to the performance that called for a “Free Palestine” and also told Jewish members of the audience that his comments regarding the Israeli government was in no way about them. The performance of “Hind’s Hall” also had related images from pro-Palestinian demonstrations and the situation in Gaza.
Kraft did not deny allegations made by Macklemore in his own statement earlier this month, but said Gillette Stadium — which his entertainment group owns — seeks to create a welcoming environment for everyone. He took issue with Macklemore’s actions at the New Jersey show and “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.”
“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” Kraft said.
The Patriots owner also said he was not trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish the suffering of Palestinians.
Kraft did not specifically reference past actions of concern from Macklemore, but many online brought up a 2014 incident in which Macklemore wore a costume that appeared to play on antisemitic tropes: a wig, a fake beard and a hooked nose. He wore it to the Grammys that year, saying at the time that he thought it would be fun to dress in disguise to talk to fans.
Macklemore apologized after the antisemitic stereotype was pointed out, saying he had been in touch with the Anti-Defamation League, an organization founded to combat antisemitism. The ADL accepted the apology at the time, saying it took him “at his word that he did not have any ill intent,” according to The Guardian .
Sheeran faced a wave of backlash over his role in the situation as some commenters felt that the singer should have taken a stance on the war or at least Macklemore’s right to speak on his opinion. All of Sheeran’s opening acts, as well as his house band, dropped out of their scheduled U.S. tour dates in solidarity with Macklemore and the Palestinian people.
The “Perfect” singer initially released a statement explaining his side of the situation and clarifying that it was not his choice to drop Macklemore. Sheeran said that his promoters, who held the contract with Macklemore, made the decision as he attempted to build bridges with venue owners.
Sheeran went on with his scheduled concert in Philadelphia on Saturday, tearfully addressing the crowd who showed up in spite of the criticism he faced.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said. “But this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
Israel launched its offensive in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and roughly 250 others were taken hostage. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza during Israel’s military campaign, including at least 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.
Sheeran acknowledged the “horrific” Oct. 7 attack on Israel by Hamas which started the war, but went on to say what has happened in Gaza as a result is “catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”
“This is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu faces new depths of isolation ahead of address to U.N. — and Israeli voters
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu faces new depths of isolation ahead of address to U.N. — and Israeli voters
articles.content_orig:
Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge
When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation.
Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
Internationally, Israel is facing growing condemnation. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.
And the US is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel, with 62% of respondents telling Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hoping he is voted out in October.
Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where mayor Zohran Mamdani has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal to assure demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.
Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.
“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”
“At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added.
Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.
“Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action.
She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”
And Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.
But in Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?”
He did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”
Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech.
A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.
With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past.
Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.
Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”
But there are multiple flashpoints now for anger from both US political parties, as well as the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.
Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not change, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”
He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.
Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement, and Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.
The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York.
Already on Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft .
Aber Kawas , who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Nethanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.
“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.
Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

articles.title_orig: Saudi-led coalition says 6 ballistic missiles are intercepted and blames Houthi rebels
articles.title_zh: Saudi-led coalition says 6 ballistic missiles are intercepted and blames Houthi rebels
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis say they have intercepted six ballistic missiles allegedly fired by the Iran-allied group towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
The missiles were destroyed on Thursday in the direction of the Saudi cities of Taif and the strategically important port of Yanbu, according to Major General Turki al-Malki, the spokesman for the Saudi-backed Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen.
Saudi air defences intercepted some of the missiles attempting to target the cities, Al-Malki told the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
There was no immediate claim of responsibility from the Houthis or other groups.
The coalition statement came as the Reuters news agency reported that an ‌‌air defence system operated by Greek ⁠⁠military ⁠⁠personnel in Saudi Arabia intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone on Thursday in ⁠⁠the wider Yanbu region, home to major oil refining facilities.
“Both were shot down,” a Greek security source told Reuters, adding that the Greek Patriot system launched two missiles but did not give details ⁠⁠on the origin of the ⁠⁠drone and the ballistic missile. A second source confirmed the information to the news agency.
Yanbu port is key to Saudi crude when shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted.
Earlier on Thursday, Saudi Arabia’s General Directorate of Civil Defence issued alerts warning of potential danger in the holy city of Mecca, the northwestern area of Tabuk, the Red Sea areas of Jeddah and Yanbu and the southern area of Taif. They later said the threat had passed and the cities were out of danger.
Last week, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Mecca , an accusation the group strongly denied, with Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi calling the Saudi claims “a heinous lie”.
It was the first time in nearly 10 years that a security alert had been activated in Mecca, home to the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest site.
The Houthis have largely attacked southern areas of Saudi Arabia.
They stepped up attacks on the kingdom after declaring a naval blockade in July, a second theatre for the US-Iran war. The Houthis also seized the whole of Yemen’s western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
Forces with Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government said on Thursday they repelled Houthi attacks along several fronts in Yemen’s southwestern Taiz governorate.
Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, said that the Houthis launched coordinated attacks on Wednesday night in a bid to reach positions on a key road connecting the Aden, Lahj and Taiz governorates.

articles.title_orig: Big business warns Trump against diesel export ban in joint letter
articles.title_zh: Big business warns Trump against diesel export ban in joint letter
articles.content_orig:
The biggest business groups in the U.S. warned President Trump against a diesel export ban this week, saying in a joint letter that such an action would prove counterproductive and raise fuel prices rather than  lower them.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Business Roundtable, National Association of Manufacturers, American Petroleum Institute and dozens of other groups told Trump that an export ban would "lead to less fuel production, tighter supplies and rising costs for American families, farmers and truckers."
"You have been asked by some to ban or limit the export of diesel to help lower prices, when in fact the opposite would occur," the groups warned in the letter sent to Trump on Wednesday.
You can download the letter here
Trump is facing growing political pressure from Republican lawmakers in farm states including Iowa to take action to lower fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Diesel cost a national average of $6.51 per gallon Thursday, $2.82 more expensive than the same period last year, according to data from AAA.
Trump said Tuesday that he has advocated for an export ban during deliberations within the administration. The remarks took the oil industry and business groups by surprise.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
Asked by Trump to explain the administration's deliberations to the press, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the White House was examining whether an export ban is "feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work."
A report on Politico Wednesday citing unnamed sources that the administration was preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days drove down diesel futures and shares of U.S. oil refiners.
But U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told The New York Times later Wednesday that "nobody wants a full blanket ban or zero exports of diesel."
"That's not being discussed," Wright told the Times. "What's being discussed is what's the most efficient way to get more diesel into the United States of America and continue maximum flows of gasoline and jet fuel and all that."
Wright, an oil industry veteran who previoulsy served as CEO of oilfield servicer Liberty Energy , has said a diesel export ban would raise U.S. gasoline prices.
Energy experts say an export ban would lead to a brief collapse in diesel prices in some U.S. regions but fuel prices would then shoot higher as refiners cut production in response to the restrictions.
Diesel prices have soared as Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries have forced Moscow to ban diesel exports. Russia was previously the second-largest diesel exporter in the world. A ban on U.S. diesel exports would remove the global market's largest source of supply.
Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, and exports through the Strait of Hormuz are constrained as Iran continues to threaten and attack tankers.

articles.title_orig: Police in Poland Arrest Ukrainian Citizen Over Fatal Stabbing
articles.title_zh: Police in Poland Arrest Ukrainian Citizen Over Fatal Stabbing
articles.content_orig:
One person was killed and four others injured when a man armed with a knife attacked clergy and worshippers at a Catholic monastery in southern Poland.
Police said the 31-year-old attacker, a Ukrainian national, went on a stabbing spree at the 17th-century Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, some 30km (19 miles) from the border with Ukraine, on Thursday morning.
The suspect, who had entered Poland from Germany earlier in the day, reportedly grabbed a knife from the abbey’s kitchen and attacked four men and one woman, including a priest in a confessional, police said.
“Three of the victims are clergy members and two are laypeople; one person has died,” said prosecutor Bozena Harasz-Wołoszyn. Two others were in “critical, life-threatening condition”.
Polish media identified the man who died as a priest. Police did not immediately confirm the identity of the deceased.
Prosecutors said the attacker was headed for a nearby border crossing back into Ukraine but instead went to the abbey.
The motive remains unclear, and doctors will assess whether he was under the influence of alcohol, Harasz-Wołoszyn said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the “murderer” would be “punished with the full severity of Polish law”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack a “horrific crime”.
“The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the law … We are shaken by this evil. Justice must be done.”
The mayor of Jaroslaw, Marcin Nazarewicz, declared a period of mourning until the end of the week.
Stabbings, particularly at religious sites, are extremely rare in Poland, one of Europe’s most Catholic countries.

articles.title_orig: Rare September Nor’easter set to slam East Coast with heavy rain, damaging winds
articles.title_zh: Rare September Nor’easter set to slam East Coast with heavy rain, damaging winds
articles.content_orig:
Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast.
Forecast models still disagree on the storm’s exact track, but one thing is clear: wherever it goes, it will hit the region hard. Forecasters have high confidence in a long-duration onshore wind event that could bring significant coastal flooding.
Coastal flood warnings and high wind watches are already in place along much of the East Coast, with more alerts likely to be issued throughout the day Thursday.
The highest rainfall totals — 2 to 3 inches or more — are most likely from Rhode Island to eastern Massachusetts.
Powerful winds, including gusts up to 50-60 mph, risk toppling power lines and trees. Small shifts in the storm’s track will determine where outages and downed trees are most likely to occur.
Coastal flooding is expected to run 1 to 3 feet above high tide, and a full moon Saturday night could intensify the tides and worsen the flooding. Waves along the coast are expected to reach 12 feet in Ocean City, New Jersey, and up to 22 feet in New England.
Moderate to major flooding is likely from North Carolina to Nantucket, Massachusetts, with southeastern Virginia — particularly the Virginia Beach-to-Norfolk area — at highest risk for major coastal inundation of 1 to 3 feet.
Meanwhile, a separate storm is already pummeling the Eastern Seaboard, generating high winds and rough surf.
In Massachusetts, residents were seen this week hauling their boats out of the bay, worried about high tides and flooding from the Nor’easter. One person told NBC News he’d been “prepping all week for both wind and water.”
One couple even changed their wedding plans because of the storm — they had been set to marry this weekend on a Massachusetts beach.
And the Boston Red Sox moved Sunday’s game — the season finale — up to Friday to avoid any weather-related delays or cancellations.
In New Jersey, crews cleared debris from storm drains and flood-prone areas as emergency management officials urged residents to prepare for the incoming storm. Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden recommended charging devices and stocking up on batteries ahead of possible power outages.
Elsewhere in the country, days of heavy rain in the Southwest have triggered major flooding, sending muddy waters sweeping through the streets of New Mexico. The El Paso, Texas, fire department said it has responded to more than 50 storm-related calls.
Off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo threatens heavy rain and flash flooding, with more than 30 inches of rain  possible in some areas. Extreme rainfall remains the storm’s biggest risk.
Nolo currently has sustained winds of 50 mph and is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday night — potentially reaching Category 3 strength. As of the latest update, the storm was about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, moving north at 2 mph.
Nolo is not expected to make direct landfall in Hawaii, but it could come close enough to bring tropical-storm-force winds to the Big Island and Maui as early as Thursday night, with hurricane-force winds possible by Friday night.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Sam Brock is an NBC News correspondent.

articles.title_orig: Week 4 college football viewer's guide: Loaded Saturday slate features 6 games between ranked teams, including Texas at Tennessee
articles.title_zh: Week 4 college football viewer's guide: Loaded Saturday slate features 6 games between ranked teams, including Texas at Tennessee
articles.content_orig:
Week 4 is the biggest weekend of the 2026 college football season.
Saturday features six matchups between teams ranked in the AP Top 25. Four of those come in the SEC and the other two are in the Big Ten. We won't filibuster any longer. Here are the games to watch this weekend.
The winner gets to be called UT for the rest of the year. The loser has to find another acronym.
It's the biggest game of young Tennessee QB Faizon Brandon's career and he's shown why he won the starting QB job as a true freshman through the first three games. Brandon has yet to throw an interception and has nine total touchdowns; he's thrown for six and rushed for three.
Two of those games have come against Furman and Kennesaw State , so it's hard to judge just how good the Volunteers offense actually is this season. But it's a promising sign that Tennessee has been able to dominate its opponents on the ground no matter who it has played. In a 45-24 win over Georgia Tech , the Vols rushed 45 times for 299 yards.
That takes pressure off Brandon; he was 10-of-21 passing for 148 yards and two scores against the Yellow Jackets. Is that run game sustainable against the Longhorns? Teams are averaging just 3.4 yards a carry against Texas this season and Ohio State had 94 yards on 31 carries.
Auburn transfer Cam Coleman hasn't caught more than four passes in a game so far the season for Texas, but he's scored twice against both Texas State and UTSA. Arch Manning is averaging under seven yards an attempt through the first three games of the season and Tennessee's opponents have thrown for just 453 yards all season.
The Rebels' status as an underdog isn't a sign of disrespect to a top-five team. Rather, it's more about how good Florida has looked through the first three weeks of Jon Sumrall's tenure.
The Gators were the clear better team in their win over Auburn as Jadan Baugh has established himself as one of the best running backs in the country. Baugh has 458 yards and eight touchdowns already this season and is averaging 8.5 yards every time he carries the ball. Teams haven't been afraid to run the ball against Ole Miss so far this season, either. Charlotte's 33 attempts are the fewest of any Ole Miss opponent and LSU rushed for 172 yards and two scores in the Rebels' 32-24 win in Week 3.
It's also a potential letdown spot for Ole Miss. The game against LSU was such a focal point since the schedule was released that it's only natural to think the Rebels won't be as up for this game. Will that be rooted in any basis in reality? We'll know on Saturday.
We may also need to wait until Saturday to know about Ole Miss RB Kewan Lacy 's status. He re-injured his surgically repaired left shoulder in the win over LSU and missed the end of the game. JT Lindsey was effective in Lacy's absence, but Ole Miss is a much better football team with its star on the field. Having Lacy out there and effective helps Trinidad Chambliss share the playmaking burden.
This game has all the potential in the world to satiate your desires for old-school football. The over/under of 38.5 is the lowest of any game offered at BetMGM in Week 4.
No one is giving up fewer points per game than Iowa through three weeks. The Hawkeyes have shut out Northern Illinois and Northern Iowa — at least Michigan doesn't have "north" in its name — and allowed 13 points to Iowa State in Week 2. Those three teams have put up just 177 yards per game.
Hank Brown has taken over as Iowa's starting quarterback after a competition with Jeremy Hecklinski that went all the way to Week 1. The former Auburn QB is 45-of-62 passing for 473 yards and three touchdowns. Those are explosive numbers compared to the passing offense that Iowa has had in recent seasons.
The biggest question may actually come at running back, where both Kamari Moulton and L.J. Phillips missed the Week 3 win. Moulton and Phillips are the Hawkeyes' top running backs. Iowa didn't need them against its FCS foe, but will need at least one available on Saturday.
Michigan's offense finally broke free in the second half of a 52-17 win over UTEP in Week 3. After scoring 30 points over the first two weeks of the season, the Wolverines nearly matched that number with four touchdowns in the third quarter alone.
Will that game be a turning point for an offense that had looked stuck for the better part of 10 quarters? There are few questions about the Michigan defense. The ceiling for the Wolverines will be entirely determined by just how good the offense can be.
Some of the luster disappeared from this game as both teams lost in Week 3. Texas A&M's home loss to Kentucky was entirely unexpected. And it wasn't a fluke, either. The Wildcats bossed the Aggies .
Texas A&M lost receiver Terry Bussey for the season with a right leg injury on the opening kickoff. That puts more pressure on Mario Craver and Isaiah Horton to be the primary playmakers for an Aggies passing game that looks to need a robust support system around quarterback Marcel Reed . Craver and Horton have combined to catch 31 of the 62 completions Reed has thrown this season and all but one of his touchdown passes.
Reed emerged as Texas A&M's quarterback in this game two seasons ago as he came off the bench to rush for three scores in a 38-23 win. This season, he's completing less than 60% of his passes.
Sam Leavitt is still looking for his first great game as LSU's starting quarterback. Leavitt has thrown at least one interception in each of the Tigers' first three games and has five interceptions to just three touchdown passes. He's supplemented that total with six rushing touchdowns, but Leavitt needs to be a better passer for the Tigers' playoff hopes to become reality.
And the playoff is going to be a central theme of this game. The loser will drop to 2-2 and likely have no path to the postseason with another loss.
This is another game with some serious playoff implications, especially for an Oregon team that already has a loss thanks to that Week 2 defeat at Oklahoma State.
Even if it'd be a victory over a .500 Oregon team, a win would be a defining one for this Big Ten version of USC. The Trojans haven't threatened to be in the top tier of the conference since making the move from the Pac-12. Yes, there was a home win over Michigan in 2025, but that Wolverines team finished with five losses.
As always, there are still questions about the USC defense. The Trojans shut out Fresno State in a dominant Week 1 performance. But they've otherwise allowed 26 points in each of the other three games and 75 points combined over the past two weeks. The 35 points Rutgers scored in Week 3 was just seven fewer than the Scarlet Knights ' combined total over the first two weeks of the season.
If Oregon's offense has the same tells that it allegedly did against Oklahoma State, former TCU coach Gary Patterson's unit can tee off. But if the Portland State game was some much-needed corrective action, the Ducks could easily be the third straight team to drop 30 or more against the Trojans. If that happens and USC still wins, QB Jayden Maiava is going to get a lot of Heisman love. Through four games, Maiava is completing 76% of his passes for 1,173 yards and 12 TDs to just one interception.
Clemson (1-) at Cal (10:30 p.m. ET Friday, ESPN): We've got some serious ACC-after-dark potential with this one. Cal CB Kingston Lopa added a fifth interception against Wagner in Week 3 and will be licking his chops at the prospect of facing freshman Tait Reynolds in his first road start. Reynolds was much better after Clemson's win over North Carolina resumed following a lengthy weather delay.
Oklahoma at No. 2 Georgia (-14) (3:30 p.m. ET, ESPN): The Sooners are big underdogs as their offense has struggled so far this season. Tackle Michael Fasusi is unlikely to play along with star defensive lineman David Stone . That could be a recipe for disaster against a Georgia team that has dominated everyone it has played so far this season. Will Gunner Stockton

articles.title_orig: A first for Ben Johnson at quarterback and more lessons from the 5 biggest NFL injuries
articles.title_zh: A first for Ben Johnson at quarterback and more lessons from the 5 biggest NFL injuries
articles.content_orig:
Five plays into the 2026 NFL season, we saw the first starting quarterback go down.
The Seattle Seahawks ' Sam Darnold suffered a glute injury against the New England Patriots , and just like that, Drew Lock was leading the defending Super Bowl champs to a comeback victory on Opening Night.
It wouldn't take much longer for more starting quarterbacks to fall.
Less than 10 minutes into his Vikings debut in Week 1, Kyler Murray was knocked out with a concussion. Week 2 saw three recent first-round quarterbacks succumb to injury: Chicago 's Caleb Williams and Washington's Jayden Daniels , the first two picks of the 2024 NFL Draft, followed by the Giants' Jaxson Dart — and each injury seemingly worse than the next.
Seattle's Sam Darnold going down on Opening Night was an omen for the early portion of the 2026 NFL season.
Along with the Atlanta Falcons , who were forced to start Cooper Rush the first two games ahead of either Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr., it's fair to say that the starting-quarterback injury epidemic is already raging after two weeks. Nearly 20% of the league has been forced to play backup QBs, with almost 90% of the regular season still remaining.
Backups clearly matter. Brock Purdy missed almost half the 2025 regular season, but Mac Jones helped keep the 49ers afloat. When C.J. Stroud missed three games last season, Texans backup Davis Mills went 3-0 in his place, keeping them in the playoff race. But when Patrick Mahomes got hurt, the drop-off to Gardner Minshew — and later Chris Oladokun — was too steep for the Chiefs to survive.
Some teams, we're finding out, have protected their most important assets better than others. Here's how we'd rank the six teams that have needed to dip into their QB reserves:
Who's the starter? Who's the backup? It's often not a pretty situation when those two questions aren't followed by easy answers.
The Falcons have the toughest situation of the lot right now, even with the most theoretical options. Tagovailoa was nominally the starter until he got hurt; Penix, the logical replacement, couldn't go the first two weeks.
That left the reins to Rush, who struggled in Baltimore last season and who did little in his two starts this season in leading the Falcons to an 0-2 start. Strand, the Division-II prospect who had an encouraging preseason, replaced Rush in Week 2 and threw a pick-6 on his first NFL pass attempt.
Clearly the hope is that the often-injured Penix can step in now, having been named Atlanta's Week 3 starter, and run with the job. The Falcons have little other hope, short of (the also often-injured) Tagovailoa returning to action.
Until proven otherwise, Kevin Stefanski has the same issue in Atlanta that he had in Cleveland : quarterback uncertainty.
With Jaxson Dart now ruled out for the season , the Giants are in a really tough spot, with no young quarterback to prepare in the wings. Winston has a wealth of experience, with 89 career starts, but as Monday's replacement performance showed, his play can be a wild experience.
Winston struggled against the Rams and has been a turnover machine in his career, with 141 of them (114 INTs, 27 lost fumbles) in 109 career outings. He's had a five-pick game and a three-fumble game. Winston also has five career 400-yard games and two five-TD, no-INT performances. You really never know what you're going to get any given week.
Head coach John Harbaugh has to find another option in case he gets too much bad Winston, with only Jake Haener currently on the practice squad. Some have floated a J.J. McCarthy trade to the Giants, but would that throw only more gas on the fire?
This pairing could arguably be higher on the list, but Bagent's concussion (which might have come on the final play Sunday) could keep him out of Monday night's game against the Philadelphia Eagles , which would give Keenum his first start — and his first regular-season action — since 2023.
Bagent has barely seen the field since Caleb Williams was drafted, but he started four games in 2023 and replaced Williams for the final two drives Sunday. His body of work is incomplete, but Bagent possesses intriguing skills and it wouldn't be shocking if he led a team at starter level for a stretch.
It's unclear how long Williams will be out, but for the first time since he came to Chicago, the Bears will have to lean on his replacements.
Lock came in cold in Week 1 and did just enough to help the Seahawks win, settling down after a few shaky patches. Then he came out guns blazing in Week 2, throwing for three TDs. Would you believe that Lock leads the NFL in passer rating through two games? He entered the season completing fewer than 60% of his career passes but is sitting at 72.7% in 2026.
If Lock, who turns 30 in November, can continue to fill in ably for the injured Darnold, it's not a stretch to think he could follow the Geno Smith post-30 path of earning his way back into a starting lineup, perhaps as a bridge option for a team that drafts a higher-round QB next spring. It appears that Lock has worked out some of the recklessness in his game and is becoming more dependable.
Milroe remains a curiosity with strong physical skills, but he's still virtually unknown. His best shot might be to continue working behind the scenes and vie for Lock's QB2 spot next season.
Wentz might be known in some circles as a bust, or as the guy whose team went on to win a Super Bowl after he got hurt. Even still, he's carved out a career for himself as an able QB2, willing and ready to jump into the fire. He did so early against the Packers when Kyler Murray got hurt, leading the Vikings to a 12-point comeback in the game's final 20 minutes. Then Wentz turned in a solid, turnover-free effort in his Week 2 start against the Bears, leading Minnesota to a shocking 9-3 win and a 2-0 start to the season.
Not bad for a guy who wasn't even part of the Vikings' starting derby in camp. His outing vs. the Bears marked 11 straight seasons with at least one start for Wentz. He'll take a seat again with Murray expected to start in Week 3, but Wentz's contributions can't be forgotten.
McCarthy, who lost the starting battle to Murray, remains an enigma. He's under contract through 2027 with a 2028 option, but the path back to being relevant for this team appears longer and more windy now.
Mariota is in some ways the gold standard of backup quarterbacks, along with the 49ers' Jones. With 82 career starts, Mariota has more experience than many current starters. He stepped in ably for Jayden Daniels in Sunday's loss to the Cowboys, looking sharp, and was competitive during Daniels' two missed stints last season.
With Daniels expected to miss 4-6 weeks with his latest left elbow injury, Mariota will be thrust back onto the saddle as he approaches his 33rd birthday. The biggest benefit is that he can run the same offense Daniels did, with little tweaking necessary.
The rookie Kaliakmanis had a strong preseason, receiving extra reps when Mariota's knee injury flared up and impressing the team with his arm talent and moxie.

Nvidia says Google’s new Gemini-infused laptops are slated to get GeForce Now support before the year is up, which is perfect because Googlebooks don’t exactly pack a ton of power.
The entire Googlebook line was officially announced on September 21, spanning across Acer, Dell, ASUS, HP, and Lenovo. Each has its own draw, but they share the same baseline 16GB of RAM, up to 32GB. Each is equipped with a touchscreen and made from “premium materials,” and they genuinely look great. What qualifies as “premium” ranges from aluminum to carbon fiber. Of course, each has the instantly iconic Glowbar somewhere on the cover, flashing when the laptop is opened or closed.
In essence, Googlebooks run Android, for better or worse. Googlebook OS is almost a parallel operating system, but it and mobile Android go hand-in-hand by design. By nature, that means Google didn’t intend to pack these with discrete graphics cards that could power most games. But that’s why GeForce Now exists, right?
Nvidia announced that GeForce Now would be coming to Googlebooks in an official capacity before the year is up. The original statement only specifies it will arrive “later this year,” which leaves a gap of around three months.
That doesn’t mean GeForce Now won’t work with Googlebooks when they become available in October. Google Chrome and even Firefox now support GeForce Now natively through the browser. That means logging into the game streaming website will present a similar experience to a fully dedicated Googlebook app.
Still, an app will likely be a better experience tailored to the hardware outfit Google and its partners pack into the new laptops.
This was expected for a couple of reasons. Google has partnered with Nvidia in the past, and Chromebooks were one of the main targets for GeForce Now in the early days. On top of that, when Googlebooks were first shown off, the majority of titles seen were via GeForce Now and not running on native hardware.

articles.title_zh: Krasnodar Region Declares State of Emergency as Ukrainian Strikes Cripple Grain Exports
articles.content_orig:
Southern Russia’s Krasnodar region has declared a state of emergency following weeks of intense Ukrainian strikes against Black Sea ports and shipping infrastructure, which have hobbled export routes and left local farms overflowing with unsold grain, authorities said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on the other's grain vessels in the Black Sea in recent months, sending global prices higher.
Krasnodar region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev signed the emergency decree on Wednesday, retroactively setting its effective date to Aug. 12. The order cites “mass attacks on logistics facilities, suspended port operations and disrupted shipping in the Azov-Black Sea basin ” as the reason for emergency measures.
In August, Ukrainian drone and missile strikes were estimated to have taken 90% of Russia’s grain export capacity in the region offline, according to industry analysts. The vast majority of the country’s agricultural shipments flow out of the Azov-Black Sea basin.
Kondratyev said many farmers in the Krasnodar region have been unable to sell their grain, leading to an oversupply that threatens to “disrupt normal living conditions for the population and cause significant material losses.”
The Krasnodar region, one of Russia’s primary agricultural hubs, has seen a very productive harvest this year, with total grain yields projected to outpace last year’s output.
Disruptions to export infrastructure have created a surplus of grain in the domestic market , leading to lower prices in Russia and unsold inventories.
The Central Bank warned this week that prolonged disruptions to grain export routes could negatively impact agricultural output in the future.
Russia is seeking to reroute its agricultural exports away from the Black Sea through its Baltic and Arctic ports, repurposing fertilizer and coal terminals to handle grain shipped by rail from southern Russia.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov held talks with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, after which Rubio said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced an interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy-related targets.
Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: How an OpenAI ‘agent’ hacked Australia’s Medicare and what that means
articles.title_zh: How an OpenAI ‘agent’ hacked Australia’s Medicare and what that means
articles.content_orig:
Australian authorities have raised the alarm after OpenAI-powered models hacked into a government health data system in June, slipping past its digital defences and accessing files without authorisation.
This is the first publicly known case of artificial intelligence (AI) “agents” – AI-powered software systems that can carry out tasks autonomously – breaking into a government website, and the latest of several AI breaches of external systems.
The disclosure comes as top AI firms warn of the risk of humans losing control of AI, calling for its development to slow to a pace that allows it to be safely regulated. Global powers must cooperate to ensure this, they have said.
A research scientist at AI firm Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, went so far as to say he believes there is a greater than 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” within a decade.
Addressing the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there is a risk of AI moving “so fast that people can no longer follow what’s happening or intervene when needed”.
“This would obviously be terrible,” he said. “And we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we will be able to keep under human control.”
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed the breach on Wednesday , saying an OpenAI agent had made its way into the public-facing medical statistics portal of Medicare, the country’s universal health insurance system, on July 18.
When OpenAI accessed the government portal while conducting research on public medical spending, Albanese said the AI agent circumvented “blocks” that should have prevented it from breaking into the portal.
“The AI agent found a way around those blocks – didn’t accept no for an answer,” said Albanese.
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the information the OpenAI agent accessed was “not particularly sensitive” and was later publicly released.
Still, Albanese called the situation “obviously unacceptable” and said Australia had relayed its “extreme concern” to OpenAI, which had failed to notify the government of the breach until September 10.
Albanese also said several other government websites may have been affected by rogue OpenAI agents, though he did not confirm any other breaches.
He added that an inquiry into the breach would look at how Australian security agencies missed it initially and whether criminal charges could be brought against OpenAI.
In a statement, OpenAI said it had “identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers” and “took actions we did not intend”.
The company said the incident occurred as its models searched for statistics on medical spending, and that they are not believed to have obtained personal medical records.
OpenAI learned of the incident in August only as it conducted a review of “misaligned model activity”, it added.
Last week, OpenAI said it had put in place a new system to monitor, probe and disclose cases of “misalignment”. That includes instances of AI models that operate “without authorisation, coordinate with other models, or evade oversight”, it said.
Yes. The Australia data breach is the latest of several instances in which AI agents belonging to OpenAI, Google or Anthropic have accessed external systems without authorisation.
In July, OpenAI reported that two of its most advanced AI models had broken out of a controlled test and hacked another AI company , Hugging Face. OpenAI later said it had detected its AI models communicating with each other and gaining internet access without authorisation months before that hack occurred.
In August, rival Meta AI said its AI model had hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. It said the model made changes to the internal systems of the hacked company, which it did not name, after accessing the public internet because of an error in the setup of its testing environment.
Maurice Chiodo, an Australian mathematician who works at Cambridge University’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, told the Reuters news agency the breach appeared to be “a significant escalation in seriousness from similar incidents we have ‌seen ‌in recent months”.
Experts say the Australia data breach highlights the growing dangers AI poses to cybersecurity as well as possible gaps in monitoring and disclosure capabilities.
“The important matter here is not what OpenAI says its agent can do, it is what the agent actually does when it hits a barrier,” Niusha Shafiabady, a professor of computational intelligence and head of the IT discipline at the Australian Catholic University, said in comments published by science news portal Scimex.
“The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision,” added Shafiabady. “Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures.”
Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, a senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney Business School, said OpenAI’s delay in reporting the breach was “concerning”.
“The incident occurred in June and only came to light months later,” said Ciriello. “Even if OpenAI did not detect the activity immediately, that still points to weaknesses in detection, escalation, and external notification.”
